The Labour Department announced today (10th) that Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) was found to have provided false information to the department during its local open recruitment when applying to import foreign labour. The department has imposed administrative sanctions, including immediately terminating the company's application and refusing to process any applications submitted by the company for the following year. According to The Collective Hong Kong's compilation of administrative sanctions cases published by the Labour Department, at least 18 companies have been penalised for violating foreign labour import regulations in the past, of which 10 are in the catering services and cleaning industries; among the 18 companies, 8 have been barred from processing foreign labour applications for one year. Reporters have inquired with the Labour Department for the latest complaint, investigation and administrative sanction figures and are awaiting a response.

Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) was subjected to administrative sanctions by the Labour Department for providing false information during its local open recruitment period.

A spokesperson for the Labour Department stated that after investigation, it was confirmed that Waso Cafe (Prince Edward) provided false information during the local open recruitment for waiters, junior chefs and dishwashers under its foreign labour import application, in violation of the rules of the "Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme". Consequently, administrative sanctions were imposed. The department has immediately terminated the company's submitted foreign labour import application and refused to process any applications submitted by the company under the Enhanced Scheme for the following year.

The department emphasised that employers importing foreign labour must strictly comply with the scheme's requirements, including prioritising the employment of suitable local workers. If employers violate labour or immigration laws, the rules of the Enhanced Scheme or standard employment contracts, the Labour Department will impose administrative sanctions, including terminating the employer's submitted applications, revoking the employer's approved quota for importing workers, and refusing to process any subsequent applications submitted by the employer.

According to Legislative Council data, since the launch of the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme in September 2023 and up to March this year, the Labour Department has received a total of 1,048 complaints, completed 287 complaint investigations, and imposed administrative sanctions on 35 employers for violating the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, occupational safety and health legislation, the Immigration Ordinance or the Enhanced Scheme's requirements.

Review of 18 Administrative Sanction Cases: Over Half Involve Catering and Cleaning Industries

Since the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme was launched in September 2023, concerns have been raised over the government's continued importation of foreign labour amid a sluggish economy and rising unemployment and underemployment rates. In August 2025, the authorities announced the first administrative sanction case, involving an employer refusing local job applicants without reasonable cause, resulting in immediate termination of the company's application and refusal to process any foreign labour applications for the following year. Later that month, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Sun Yuk-han stated that the foreign labour mechanism would not be tolerated for abuse, and that in the future, depending on the severity of individual cases and public concern, the names of non-compliant employers would be disclosed where practicable.

The Collective Hong Kong has compiled cases of administrative sanctions publicly disclosed by the Labour Department. Including Waso Cafe (Prince Edward), which was sanctioned today, the Labour Department has imposed administrative sanctions on at least 18 employers for violating foreign labour import regulations, of which 6 companies are in the catering services industry and 4 are cleaning service companies; the main reason for most sanctions was refusing to hire local job applicants without reasonable cause, followed by providing false information. Among them, companies that refused to hire local workers were mostly barred from applying for foreign labour for the following two years, while some companies that provided false information were mostly suspended from processing applications for one year.

In two cases, Sheung Yuen Chinese Restaurant Limited, which operates Sheung Yuen Chinese Restaurant, and Jantias Group Limited, which operates Yung Yuen, were found to have dismissed local workers after hiring foreign labour. They were barred from submitting applications for the following two years, and their approved foreign labour import approvals were immediately revoked. However, for the 11 foreign worker quotas already used by Sheung Yuen Chinese Restaurant, the foreign workers already on duty were allowed to continue working in Hong Kong.

According to Legislative Council data, the Labour Department stated that up to March this year, it had received a total of 1,048 complaints, completed 287 complaint investigations, and imposed administrative sanctions on 35 employers for violating the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, occupational safety and health legislation, the Immigration Ordinance or the Enhanced Scheme's requirements. The Collective Hong Kong has inquired with the Labour Department for the latest complaint, investigation and administrative sanction figures and is awaiting a response.
